rationale: Across reported cohorts of Jaberi-Elahi syndrome (caused by biallelic variants in GTPBP2), neuroimaging shows marked phenotypic variability. While thinning or hypoplasia/agenesis of the corpus callosum is a frequent finding, it is not an obligate feature. Several molecularly confirmed cases demonstrate other patterns such as periventricular white matter abnormalities, delayed myelination, or cerebellar atrophy without callosal dysgenesis. Therefore, callosal agenesis/hypogenesis occurs in only a subset of patients, and its absence does not exclude Jaberi-Elahi syndrome in individuals presenting with core features such as microcephaly, developmental delay, cerebellar involvement, and ectodermal findings.

evidence.text: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome exhibits phenotypic heterogeneity including variable neuroimaging findings. A 4-month-old infant with confirmed homozygous pathogenic GTPBP2 frameshift variant presented with periventricular white matter abnormalities on MRI without reported callosal agenesis or hypogenesis.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact penetrance of corpus callosum hypoplasia/agenesis on high-resolution MRI when stratified systematically across all 28+ known Jaberi-Elahi syndrome cases?
new_directions.rationale: Existing cohort syntheses evaluate symptoms like sparse hair and motor delay systematically (e.g., 26/28), but exact numerators and denominators for corpus callosum dysgenesis vs. isolated cerebellar atrophy remain pooled under general neuroimaging summaries.

new_directions.question_text: Does corpus callosum thinning in GTPBP2 deficiency represent progressive white matter loss / secondary atrophy over time rather than primary dysgenesis?
new_directions.rationale: Age-related neurodegeneration and brain iron accumulation occur in older patients, raising the question of whether callosal thinning is acquired secondary to progressive axonal loss rather than true congenital agenesis.
